briefing.question: Order versus liberty in the franchise: is it worse to count one ineligible ballot or to block one eligible voter, and who should bear the burden of proof?
briefing.agreed: Only citizens vote; whoever accuses a voter must prove it.
briefing.split: Blackstone, Beccaria, proof first; Hamilton, laws made in advance; Locke, both wrongs; Madison.

briefing.question: Leadership and responsibility: does a leader own the outcomes of decisions made in his name, and does loyalty require silence or candor?
briefing.agreed: A leader owns his decisions; loyalty includes candor.
briefing.split: Aristotle, common good; Machiavelli, results and alibis; Cicero; Burke, judgment; Aquinas, mercy.

briefing.question: The nature of poverty and the dignity of the poor: is poverty mainly a matter of circumstance or of habits and formation, and what does a society owe those in need?
briefing.agreed: The poor are owed help, given as to equals.
briefing.split: Smith, habits and circumstance; Rousseau, arrangements; Tocqueville, association; Aquinas; Leo XIII.

briefing.question: What makes an economic order just: equal outcomes, fair rules, or the freedom to try?
briefing.agreed: Hard work should buy a stake of one's own.
briefing.split: Locke, enough left; Marx, estrangement; Leo XIII, just wage; Mill, reform; Hayek, no planner; Smith.

briefing.question: Is money speech? Where does free expression end and the corruption of self-government begin?
briefing.agreed: Free speech matters; bought exclusivity corrupts.
briefing.split: Madison, control effects; Milton, no licenser; Mill, lower costs; Aristotle, the middle; Tocqueville.

briefing.question: What is a university for: the pursuit of truth through contested ideas, or the transmission of settled knowledge? And who should guard it?
briefing.agreed: One-sided learning fails; quotas by party control.
briefing.split: Mill, more argument; Newman, scholars; Aristotle, public aims; Smith, students; Tocqueville, conformity.

briefing.question: What makes something human work: the result, or the effort, intention and skill behind it?
briefing.agreed: Tools can give results without forming the maker.
briefing.split: Plato, inner work; Aristotle, practice; Ruskin, thinking maker; Tolstoy, sincerity; Benjamin, ownership.

briefing.question: What do the living owe the dead, and is there room for purification after death, or is grace finished at the cross?
briefing.agreed: The dead are owed remembrance; grace is not for sale.
briefing.split: Augustine, prayer helps; Francis, sister death; Luther, no pardons; Calvin, the cross; Newman, development.

briefing.question: Faith in public life: should a candidate's religious teaching be fair game, and what separates scrutiny of conviction from a religious test?
briefing.agreed: No law bars a candidate for faith; voters may weigh.
briefing.split: Madison, test versus judgment; Washington, no bigotry; Locke, equal protection; Augustine; Williams.

briefing.question: The role of faith in public life: is political engagement an obligation of love, or a temptation that compromises the church's witness?
briefing.agreed: Seek the city's good; the church is no interest group.
briefing.split: Augustine, pilgrim vote; Calvin, calling; Tertullian, distance; Leo XIII; Kuyper; Tocqueville, authority.

briefing.question: Heavenly citizenship and earthly loyalty: is patriotism a natural virtue, or a rival to the believer's first allegiance?
chairs: Author of the Epistle to Diognetus
briefing.agreed: God first; love of homeland is not wrong in itself.
briefing.split: Augustine, no idolatry; Diognetus, sojourners; Aquinas, piety; Cicero, ordered; Burke, a lovely country.

sittings.headline: Supreme Court refuses to make California set aside 20,000 flagged mail ballots
sittings.question: Order versus liberty in the franchise: is it worse to count one ineligible ballot or to block one eligible voter, and who should bear the burden of proof?

setup.text: On the eve of the midterms the Supreme Court, in a one-line unsigned order with no noted dissents, denied the Justice Department's emergency request to make California separate mail ballots from about 20,000 people the administration flagged as likely noncitizens. Lower courts had already refused, and separately a federal judge on Friday barred federal agencies from demanding that election officials anywhere segregate ballots, purge voters or halt processing.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Blackstone speaks first because the report names his ratio, that it is better ten guilty escape than one innocent suffer, and because he also wrote that a free state must carefully regulate who votes, so both sides can claim him. Beccaria wrote the classic case that no one may be treated as guilty before a judge decides, and also that prevention beats punishment, the two halves of tonight's dispute. Hamilton is seated for Federalist 59 and the Elections Clause, which the report names. Locke wrote that a people needs a settled, known law and known judges, the core of the burden-of-proof argument. Madison wrote that the definition of the suffrage is fundamental and designed the division of powers the Purcell habit protects. Hobbes, seated on this question two nights ago, is left off so the table can turn to burden of proof rather than sovereign force. Magna Carta is a charter rather than a thinker, so its lawful-judgment clause is carried by Blackstone and Locke. The Justices, the department, California officials and the voters on the list are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: order versus liberty in the franchise. Is it worse to count one ineligible ballot or to block one eligible voter, and who should bear the burden of proof? The report gives one side as saying only citizens may vote, the window to check closes for good once envelopes are opened, and courts that will not even pause to verify are choosing speed over integrity. The other side says California checked a sample of the list and found many citizens on it, the administration never explained how the list was built, and setting aside lawful voters' ballots the day before an election would disenfranchise citizens and hand Washington control of a state's count. We decide nothing tonight about the list itself. Blackstone, you begin.

turn.text: Blackstone gives the ratio; I gave the principle under it. “A man cannot be called guilty before sentence has been passed on him by a judge, nor can society deprive him of its protection till it has been decided that he has broken the condition on which it was granted.” (Of Crimes and Punishments, ch. XII) A citizen whose ballot is set aside on the strength of a list has been treated as guilty before any judge has looked at her case, and that is exactly what the lower courts and now the high court declined to permit.

XLI) Once an envelope is opened, the ballot cannot be pulled back, so prevention is the only remedy that works at all. My answer is that prevention must be proportioned to the evidence: check the names that can be checked, one by one and quickly, and refer any proven case to prosecution afterward. A sweeping hold on everyone listed is punishment wearing the mask of prevention.

turn.text: Beccaria guards the individual; the report names my paper, so let me guard the Union. I argued that “an exclusive power of regulating elections for the national government, in the hands of the State legislatures, would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy.” (Federalist No. 59) Federal elections are not the private property of any state, and the nation has a real interest in who chooses its Congress.

turn.text: But read what remedy I actually defended. The framers left elections to the states in the first instance, and “they have reserved to the national authority a right to interpose, whenever extraordinary circumstances might render that interposition necessary to its safety.” (Federalist No. 59) That is a reserve power exercised by Congress through general laws, made in advance, for extraordinary circumstances. It is not an executive department asking a court, on the eve of the vote, to halt part of one state's count on a list it has not explained. The interest is national; the method must be lawful and settled before the game begins, which is the sense in the judges' habit of not changing rules on the eve of an election.

A party that cannot say which principle it shares apart from its leader has become a following, and a following cannot correct itself.

Milton's Areopagitica, named in the report, is the founding plea for unlicensed speech. opening.text: Tonight's subject: is money speech? Where does free expression end and the corruption of self-government begin? Walter Benjamin is named for the essay on art in the age of mechanical reproduction; his work is in copyright translation, so he is paraphrased. William Morris, close to Ruskin on craft, is left off as a second voice for the same view. The post's author and the creators replying are context only.

opening.text: Tonight's subject: what makes something human work: the result, or the effort, intention and skill behind it? The other side says every new tool, from the camera to the synthesizer, was mocked this way, that AI lets people with ideas but no training finally make things, and that the sneer is gatekeeping dressed as standards. sittings.why_these_chairs: Augustine speaks first because his account of the peace of Babylon is the classic Christian reading of Jeremiah's command to seek the welfare of the city, which the report names. Calvin wrote that Christians live under two governments and owe prayer and duty to the civil one. Tertullian gives the earliest Christian voice for principled distance from affairs of state, close to the Anabaptist tradition the report names. Leo XIII wrote both that Catholics should take part in public affairs and that the Church must never be tied to a party. Kuyper is named for sphere sovereignty and engaged citizenship; his lectures are paraphrased because they were not verified against a fetched text tonight. Tocqueville observed that religion in America gained influence by staying out of government. H. Richard Niebuhr's Christ and Culture, named in the report, is in copyright and is described by the moderator; Michael Sattler and the Schleitheim Confession are left off because their text was not fetched, and Tertullian carries the separatist case. opening.text: Tonight's subject: is political engagement an obligation of love, or a temptation that compromises the church's witness? The report gives one side as those urging turnout: Christians are citizens with a duty to love their neighbors through good laws, staying home is itself a political choice, and abstaining hands the culture to others. The other side says the church's hope is not in elections, tying the gospel to partisan turnout makes it look like one more interest group, and the deeper witness is how believers treat people, including opponents. The report sets two texts side by side. Jeremiah wrote to the exiles: “And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.” (Jeremiah 29:7) And Jesus told Pilate: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36) Niebuhr's Christ and Culture later mapped the options as Christ against, above, or transforming culture. Augustine, you begin.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Augustine speaks first because the report names the City of God and its pilgrims who still seek the earthly city's peace. The anonymous Epistle to Diognetus is named for its picture of Christians who live in their own countries as sojourners; its author is unknown and is seated by the work. Aquinas is named for the principle that grace perfects nature rather than destroying it, and his question on piety names one's country as a debt after God. Cicero gave the classical account of love of country as the widest of natural loves, which Aquinas drew on. Burke wrote of the little platoon as the root of public affection and of a country that must be lovely to be loved. Modern Christian nationalism and its critics are left to the users in the report; the account and its repliers are context only.

The report gives one side as those agreeing that the New Testament makes the church a new people from every tribe and tongue, so a Christian's first and deepest belonging cannot be to any ethnicity or state, and blurring that leads toward idolatry of nation. turn.text: Augustine speaks of a pilgrim city; I described what pilgrims look like when they stay home. “They dwell in their own countries, but simply as sojourners. As citizens, they share in all things with others, and yet endure all things as if foreigners. Every foreign land is to them as their native country, and every land of their birth as a land of strangers.” (Epistle to Diognetus, ch. 5) We did not leave our countries or refuse their customs, their food or their duties. We simply could not treat any of them as final.

turn.text: I placed love of country within the virtue of piety: “Consequently man is debtor chiefly to his parents and his country, after God.” (Summa Theologica II-II, Q. 101, Art. 1) That is a debt of gratitude, owed because our country gave us birth and nourishment. Notice the order: after God. Diognetus is right that nothing earthly is final, and the post's critics are right that the debt is real. Piety toward one's country becomes a vice only when it outranks God or turns into contempt for other peoples.

turn.text: Cicero gives the circles; I would say where love of them begins. “To be attached to the subdivision, to love the little platoon we belong to in society, is the first principle (the germ, as it were) of public affections.” (Reflections on the Revolution in France) We learn to love mankind by first loving particular people and places. A faith that asked us to skip that step would ask us to love an abstraction.
